warmup.q: The nightly copy from the opening runs at a steady 7.5 Mbit/s over a quiet 1 Gbit/s line, and a message takes 70 ms to get there and back. What is the most likely limit?
options: Some packets get lost on the way, and resending them keeps slowing the copy down
The receiving computer only has room for 64 KB at a time, and the sender can't send more than that before hearing back
The disk on the backup computer is too slow
The packets are small, so their address labels use up most of the line
warmup.why: 64 KB every 70 ms is 0.94 MB a second, which is 7.5 Mbit/s: the speed is exactly the room divided by the round trip. To fill 1 Gbit/s at 70 ms, 8.75 MB would have to be on the way at once. Lost packets slow TCP down too, but they make the speed jump up and down rather than sit flat at one value; the third section shows why. Any working disk writes far faster than 0.94 MB a second. And headers are 40 of every 1,500 bytes, under 3%.

sections.h: The speed limit of one connection: one window per round trip
sections.html:
In UDP and the sockets API, we built the simplest reliable sender: send one message, wait for its acknowledgment (an ACK), then send the next. That's called stop and wait, and its cost is easy to work out. Each message takes one round trip, the time for a message to go there and an answer to come back. Across 70 ms, about the round trip between the two coasts of the United States, that's 14 messages a second, however fast the line is.

Picture a warehouse that sends parcels by van to a shop a day's drive away. If the dispatcher sends one van and waits for the driver to come back with a signed note before sending the next, the shop gets one vanload every two days. A wider road changes nothing. The fix is to let several vans be on the road at once.

TCP does the same with bytes. The sender may send up to one window of bytes that haven't been acknowledged yet, without waiting. As ACKs come back, the window moves forward along the stream of bytes, and more bytes may go. That's the sliding window. In van terms, the window is how many vanloads may be out at once, and each signed note frees a place for one more.

So the speed limit of one connection is easy to write down:

throughput <= window / round-trip time

Throughput is how much data arrives per second. Lines are measured in bits per second, and a byte is 8 bits, so 1 Gbit/s (a billion bits a second) is 125 MB a second. A 64 KB window across 70 ms moves at most 64 KB every 70 ms: 0.94 MB a second, or 7.5 Mbit/s, on a line that could carry 1 Gbit/s. That's the opening's nightly copy, to the decimal.

Turn the formula around, and you get how big the window must be to fill a line: its bandwidth (what it can carry per second) times the round trip. That's the bandwidth-delay product (BDP). 1 Gbit/s times 70 ms is 8.75 MB that must be in flight, sent and not yet acknowledged, all the time. Inside one building, with a 0.5 ms round trip, the same line needs only 62 KB. Long, fast paths need big windows. Short paths hardly care.

Who decides the window? Two parties, for two different reasons, and the next two sections take one each. The receiver says how much room it has: the receive window. The sender guesses how much the network can carry without overflowing: the congestion window. At every moment, the sender uses the smaller of the two.

Every TCP segment (TCP's name for a packet) starts with a header, a few fields of numbers, and one of those fields got in the way. The window field is 16 bits, so it can say at most 65,535 bytes, which was plenty in 1981. Window scaling (RFC 7323, one of the documents that define TCP) fixes that with an option in the SYN, the first segment of a connection. In the capture from TCP connections: handshake, states and TIME_WAIT, wscale 7 meant "multiply every window I announce by 2^7 = 128". So the win 502 in that capture's ACKs was really 502 x 128 = 64,256 bytes. The option only counts if both SYNs carry it, so a firewall (a device that filters traffic) that strips TCP options can hold a connection at 64 KB for good.

The receive window can never be bigger than the receiver's socket buffer. A socket is what the kernel, the core of the operating system, gives a program for one end of a connection, and its receive buffer is memory set aside for arriving bytes. So a program can cap the window by setting that buffer's size, with the SO_RCVBUF option. The Try it below does that across a 50 ms round trip, and the speed follows the window. Next, we'll look at the first of the two parties, the receiver.

try.title: Throughput follows the window
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. It's a small Linux machine that runs inside Docker, with network tools installed. The first two lines make its loopback (the machine's connection to itself) behave like a long network path: a largest packet of 1,500 bytes, and 25 ms of delay each way from netem, a Linux feature that delays or drops packets on purpose. ping should show a round trip of about 50 ms.

Window.java sends as fast as it can for 2 seconds, four times: with receive buffers of 16 KB, 64 KB and 1 MB, and once with the kernel left to size the buffer itself. Predict the first two speeds from window / round trip before you run it.

On a Mac, ./gradlew :net:demo -Pmain=sfz.net.l08.demo.Window -Pargs='16 64 0' runs it without the added delay. The round trip is then a few microseconds, so even the 16 KB window moved about 100 MB/s in one run: a small window only hurts on a long path.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: ip link set lo mtu 1500 tc qdisc add dev lo root netem delay 25ms ping -c 3 -q 127.0.0.1 | tail -1 java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l08/demo/Window.java 16 64 1024 0 sysctl net.core.rmem_max net.ipv4.tcp_rmem

try.expect:
From one run:

rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 51.992/55.165/57.534/2.332 ms
receive buffer 16 KB:     0.98 MB in 2.4 s =   0.42 MB/s
receive buffer 64 KB:     3.67 MB in 2.3 s =   1.62 MB/s
receive buffer 1024 KB:   9.11 MB in 2.3 s =   3.88 MB/s
receive buffer auto:     93.32 MB in 2.1 s =  45.52 MB/s
net.core.rmem_max = 212992
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096	131072	6291456

16 KB and 64 KB grow in step: about 23 KB and 90 KB per 55 ms round trip. They aren't exactly 16 and 64, because Linux doubles the buffer size you ask for and keeps part of it for its own bookkeeping. 1 MB isn't 16 times faster than 64 KB, because Linux quietly caps a buffer size you set yourself at net.core.rmem_max, 212,992 bytes here. Left alone, the kernel grows the buffer while the transfer runs (that's called autotuning, up to the 6 MB in the last number of tcp_rmem) and reaches 45 MB/s. Setting the buffer by hand turned autotuning off. Speeds vary with the machine; the ratios don't.

aside.title: Why not make every window huge?
aside.html: Memory, for one thing. A receive window is backed by buffer memory, and a server with 10,000 connections would need 87.5 GB to give each one 8.75 MB. That's why Linux grows a buffer only for a connection that needs it (autotuning). The congestion window isn't yours to set at all: it's the sender's guess about a road it shares with everyone else. Sending more than the road holds only fills a router's queue and loses packets, as the third section shows.

sections.h: Flow control: the receiver says how much room it has
sections.html:
Every ACK in the capture from TCP connections: handshake, states and TIME_WAIT had a win field, the window. The receiver fills it with the free space in its socket's receive buffer. Arriving bytes wait in that buffer until the program calls read() and takes them. So the receive window is a running report on how fast the receiving program reads: "I can take this many more bytes".

In the van picture, the shop has a stockroom, and each signed note says how much shelf space is still free. If the staff unpack as fast as vans arrive, the space stays open. If they stop unpacking, the shelves fill, and the notes say so.

The same happens to a program that stops reading. Maybe Java has paused it to clean up memory it no longer uses (garbage collection), or it's waiting on a slow database, or it's busy with other work. The buffer fills. The window shrinks with every ACK, and at last the receiver announces win 0. The sender must stop. Its own bytes pile up in its send buffer, and once that's full too, the sending program's write() blocks: it waits until there's room. This chain is flow control. It's also the simplest kind of backpressure, a slow receiver slowing down a fast sender. The slow side's kernel holds back the fast side's program, without a line of your code.

A stopped sender has to find out when the window opens again. The receiver does send a window update once its program reads, but that update could be lost. Then both sides would wait forever, each politely waiting for the other. So the sender keeps a persist timer, a clock that reminds it to ask, and sends a tiny probe now and then, and the answer carries the current window.

Two columns of ss -tn, the Linux command that lists connections, show where the bytes are waiting. On a connected socket, Recv-Q is bytes the kernel has received that the program hasn't read yet. Send-Q is bytes the program has written that the other side hasn't acknowledged. A big Recv-Q means a slow reader on this machine. A big Send-Q means the other side reads slowly, or the network delivers slowly.

In the Try it below, a paused reader's kernel holds about 6 MB, and the sender's kernel holds another 2.7 MB. That's almost 9 MB that the sending program wrote "successfully" and nobody has read. UDP and the sockets API warned that a successful send only means your own kernel took the bytes. Here's that warning with a size attached.

A successful write() means your kernel has the bytes. It says nothing about the reader. Flow control protects the receiver, and that's all it does. It knows nothing about the roads and routers in between, and they're the next section's problem.

try.title: Pause the reader
steps: Start a fresh lab box. The first lines start a receiver (nc -l, which listens and throws everything away) and a sender that writes 100 MB of zeros to it over 127.0.0.1, the machine's address for itself.
kill -STOP freezes the receiving program, the way a long pause freezes a Java program, but its socket stays open. Predict Recv-Q and Send-Q three seconds later.
kill -CONT lets it run again, and the transfer finishes.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: nc -l 127.0.0.1 9000 > /dev/null & reader=$! sleep 0.5 head -c 100000000 /dev/zero | nc -N 127.0.0.1 9000 & sleep 0.3; kill -STOP $reader; echo "reader paused" sleep 3 ss -tn '( sport = :9000 or dport = :9000 )' ss -tin dport = :9000 | grep -oE 'rwnd_limited:[^ ]+|notsent:[0-9]+' kill -CONT $reader; echo "reader resumed" sleep 0.5 ss -tn '( sport = :9000 or dport = :9000 )'

try.expect:
From one run:

reader paused
State Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
ESTAB 6208110 0           127.0.0.1:9000     127.0.0.1:47022
ESTAB 0       2770322     127.0.0.1:47022    127.0.0.1:9000
rwnd_limited:2960ms(92.5%)
notsent:2770322
reader resumed
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:PortProcess

The receiving socket (local port 9000) holds 6.2 MB its program hasn't read, the most its autotuned buffer allows. The sending socket holds 2.7 MB of Send-Q, none of it even sent (notsent), because the window is 0. rwnd_limited is the kernel's own diagnosis: for 92.5% of the connection's life, the receive window held the sender back. Behind that, nc's write() was blocked. Half a second after the reader resumed, everything had drained and both sockets were gone.

sections.h: Congestion control: the sender guesses what the road can take
sections.html:
The receive window says nothing about the path between the two machines. Somewhere on that path is the slowest link, the bottleneck. In front of it sits a router (a machine that passes packets on) with a queue, a waiting area for packets. Say the link carries 20 Mbit/s and the queue holds 100 packets. Send faster than 20 Mbit/s and the queue fills. Once it's full, the router drops every packet that doesn't fit.

On the road, the bottleneck is a narrow bridge with a small car park in front of it. Vans that arrive faster than the bridge lets them over wait in the car park. When the car park is full, the next vans are turned away, and their parcels are lost.

A sender that answers loss by resending at the same speed only makes the queue worse. In October 1986, the early internet did exactly that. The speed between two university sites at Berkeley fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s (bits, not kilobits), a congestion collapse. Van Jacobson's fix (no relation to our vans), congestion control, has been part of TCP since the late 1980s.

The sender keeps a second window, the congestion window (cwnd): its own guess of how much the path can carry. It never has more than the smaller of cwnd and the receive window in flight. Nobody tells it the right number, so it tries, and treats loss as the signal:

  • Slow start. A new connection starts small, at 10 segments on Linux (RFC 6928), about 14 KB. Each ACK adds one segment, so the window doubles every round trip: 10, 20, 40, 80.
  • Congestion avoidance. Above a threshold called ssthresh (slow-start threshold), growth turns gentle: one more segment per round trip.
  • Loss. Three duplicate ACKs, the receiver repeating the same ACK number, say one segment is missing while later ones still arrive. The sender resends it at once, which is called fast retransmit, and halves the window. If nothing at all comes back for a whole retransmission timeout (the resend timer from UDP and the sockets API), that's worse news. The window drops to 1, and slow start begins again.

The pattern has a name: additive increase, multiplicative decrease. Add one at a time, cut in half at once. Over time, the window draws a sawtooth. It climbs until the queue overflows, halves, and climbs again. Step through it below, on a path that holds 100 segments.

Linux doesn't run this plain version, called Reno. Its default since 2006 is CUBIC (RFC 9438), which is also the default on Windows and on Apple's systems. After a loss, CUBIC cuts the window to 70%, not 50%. Then it grows the window along a cubic curve of the time since the loss. The curve rises fast at first, goes flat near the window where the loss happened, then rises faster again to look for more. Because it counts in seconds rather than round trips, a connection to a faraway machine isn't left behind by a nearby one.

BBR, from Google, works differently. It measures the bottleneck's speed and the shortest round trip, and paces its sending to match, instead of waiting for loss. Its current version, BBRv3, is still an Internet-Draft (a proposal, not yet an RFC), and the lab box's kernel offers only reno and cubic.

Loss costs speed fast. With 50 ms of delay on the lab network, a 10 MB download took about 2 seconds with no loss. With 1% of packets dropped, it took about 20 seconds (three runs of each). One lost packet in a hundred made it ten times slower.

So far, we've moved big files. The last section turns to the opposite problem: many tiny messages.

try.title: Watch the kernel's congestion window
steps: From the labs folder, with the lab network up (docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d, two small Linux machines called client and peer), start a receiver on client that throws data away. Then open a shell on peer: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer bash.

On peer, the netem rule turns its link into a bottleneck: 50 ms of delay, 20 Mbit/s, and a queue of 100 packets. The path holds about 186 segments: 86 on the way (20 Mbit/s times 50 ms is 125 KB) plus 100 waiting in the queue. ip tcp_metrics flush all makes Linux forget what it learned about this path from earlier connections.
Send 15 MB, and read cwnd and ssthresh from ss -ti every 250 ms. Predict where the first loss happens, and what CUBIC does after it.

code.title: first in labs/, then on peer
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec -d client sh -c 'nc -l -p 9100 > /dev/null' # on peer ip tcp_metrics flush all tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 50ms rate 20mbit limit 100 head -c 15000000 /dev/zero | nc -N 10.10.1.10 9100 & for i in $(seq 0 24); do printf '%5d ms ' $((i*250)); ss -tin dst 10.10.1.10:9100 | grep -oE ' (cwnd|ssthresh):[0-9]+' | tr -d '\n'; echo; sleep 0.25; done wait tc -s qdisc show dev eth0 | head -2 tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

Slow start took the window from 10 to 359 in half a second, far past the 186 segments the path holds. So the queue overflowed, and the losses brought ssthresh down to 176. CUBIC then grew the window again, lost a few more segments near 194, and cut to 138, about 70% of that. After that it climbed quickly, then flattened out at 168, a little below where it last lost packets: that's CUBIC's plateau, the flat top of its curve. netem dropped 130 of 10,363 packets, and nc never noticed, because TCP resent every one. Your numbers will differ from run to run, but the shape stays.

video.title: How TCP feels for a speed limit nobody tells it

sections.h: Small messages: Nagle's rule meets the delayed ACK
sections.html:
The last problem is the opposite of a big transfer: many tiny segments. Type one character into a remote shell (a command window on another machine), and TCP could send a 41-byte packet to carry it. That's 1 byte of data and 40 bytes of headers, a van sent out to deliver one envelope.

In 1984, John Nagle proposed a simple rule (RFC 896): while some sent data is still unacknowledged, don't send another small segment. Collect the small writes, and send them together when the ACK arrives. Full-size segments still go at once. A burst of tiny writes then costs one packet per round trip instead of one per write. In the van picture, the dispatcher won't send out a half-empty van while the last one hasn't reported back.

The receiving side has a saving of its own, the delayed ACK (RFC 1122). Instead of acknowledging each segment at once, the receiver waits a little, hoping to put the ACK on data it's about to send anyway, such as the answer. RFC 1122 caps the wait at 500 ms, and Linux waits at least 40 ms. That's the shop that waits to sign for a delivery until it has something to send back with the driver.

Each rule makes sense on its own. Together, they stall for 40 ms on a pattern that request-and-answer code uses all the time: write, write, read. A client writes a 12-byte header, then a 100-byte body, then waits for the reply.

  1. The header goes out at once: nothing was unacknowledged.
  2. The body is small and the header isn't ACKed yet, so Nagle holds the body back.
  3. The server has half a request and nothing to send, so it delays its ACK, hoping for something to put it on.
  4. 40 ms later, the delayed-ACK timer fires. The ACK reaches the client, Nagle releases the body, and the server answers.

Each side waits for the other, and every request now takes 40 ms plus its round trips. The Try it runs on a path whose round trip is a few microseconds. It measures a median (the middle value) of 42 ms per request with Nagle on, and well under 1 ms with it off. The client measures 42 ms, while the server's own log would say it answered in under a millisecond. Both are right: the missing time is spent with the body sitting in the client's own kernel.

There are two fixes, and both belong in the client. Write each message with one write(): build it in a buffer, or wrap the stream in a BufferedOutputStream and flush once, so there's never a second small segment to hold back. Or turn Nagle off with TCP_NODELAY: socket.tcpNoDelay = true, or StandardSocketOptions.TCP_NODELAY on a channel. Never send one request in small pieces with Nagle on. Write it once, or turn Nagle off. Many networking libraries turn TCP_NODELAY on for you. Among them are Netty, a popular Java networking library, and the Java clients for Kafka and PostgreSQL, two widely used data programs. A plain java.net.Socket doesn't.

One more delay hides inside every TCP connection: head-of-line blocking, the first in line holding up everyone behind it. TCP hands bytes to the program only in order. If segment 7 is lost and segments 8 to 40 arrive, the receiver's kernel holds all of them back until the resent 7 arrives, at least one round trip later. That happens even when 8 to 40 belong to other requests sharing the connection. HTTP/2, a newer version of the web's language, sends many requests over one connection, so one lost packet stalls them all. The lesson HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over QUIC shows how HTTP/3 avoids it.

try.title: Measure the 40 ms stall
steps: In the lab box, read labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l08/demo/Nagle.java. A client sends 50 requests over one connection on 127.0.0.1, each as two writes (a 12-byte header, then a 100-byte body), and reads a 2-byte reply after each. It runs once with Nagle on, which is Java's default, and once with TCP_NODELAY.
A round trip on 127.0.0.1 takes a few microseconds. Predict the median time per request for both runs anyway, then run it.

On a Mac, ./gradlew :net:demo -Pmain=sfz.net.l08.demo.Nagle runs the same code, but the stall may not show at all: macOS has its own delayed-ACK rules, and in one run both medians were under 1 ms. Linux machines are where you'll meet it.
try.expect:
From one run:

TCP_NODELAY false median  41.67 ms   slowest  48.52 ms   all 50 took  2065 ms
TCP_NODELAY true  median   0.29 ms   slowest   0.82 ms   all 50 took    14 ms

With Nagle on, nearly every request waited for one delayed-ACK timer, about 40 ms, on a path with a round trip of microseconds: 50 requests took 2 seconds instead of 14 ms. The first request of a connection is usually fast, because Linux ACKs at once for a while after a connection opens (quick-ACK mode). From the second request on, the stall is regular. The exact milliseconds vary a little from run to run; the 40 ms floor doesn't.

refs.title: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks (Nagle)
Julia Evans: Why you should understand (a little) about TCP

opening:
Every night, the payments company copies the day's records, a 2 GB file, to a backup computer in another country. The line between them carries 1 Gbit/s, a billion bits a second, so the copy should take about 16 seconds. It takes 36 minutes, at a steady 7.5 Mbit/s, night after night.

The tempting fix is a faster line. Internet plans are sold in megabits per second, so that number feels like the speed. But this line is almost idle. Something else holds the copy back, and a faster line would change nothing.

In TCP connections: handshake, states and TIME_WAIT, we opened and closed a connection, and found that an open connection says nothing about how fast we may send. In this lesson, we'll find the speed limit of one connection and meet the two windows that set it, one for the receiver and one for the network. Then we'll chase a 40 ms delay that hides in small messages. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a nightly copy that took 36 minutes on a line that could do it in 16 seconds. The line was fine. The window was 64 KB, and one window per 70 ms round trip is 7.5 Mbit/s, whatever the line can carry.

On a Linux machine, run ss -tin while something downloads, and find cwnd, mss and rtt in the output. Multiply the window by the segment size, divide by the round trip, and compare the result with the speed you see.

Next, we'll step back to the moment before any connection opens. A program knows a name, such as example.com, and needs an address. Who tells it, and how long does that answer stay true?

compare.title: One request on the wire, with Nagle on and with TCP_NODELAY

a.label: Nagle on (the default)
a.title: tcpdump -ttt, request 2 of 50
a.html:
00:00:00.000080 client > server: [P.] seq 113:125     12-byte header
 00:00:00.040677 server > client: [.]  ack 125         delayed ACK, 40 ms later
 00:00:00.000041 client > server: [P.] seq 125:225     100-byte body, released
 00:00:00.000011 server > client: [.]  ack 225
 00:00:00.000138 server > client: [P.] seq 3:5         the 2-byte reply

b.label: TCP_NODELAY
b.title: tcpdump -ttt, request 2 of 50
b.html:
00:00:00.000135 client > server: [P.] seq 113:125     12-byte header
 00:00:00.000036 client > server: [P.] seq 125:225     100-byte body, right behind it
 00:00:00.000071 server > client: [.]  ack 225
 00:00:00.000063 server > client: [P.] seq 3:5         the 2-byte reply

compare.note: Both come from recording the Nagle demo with tcpdump on 127.0.0.1 (-ttt prints the time since the previous line; addresses shortened and options trimmed). The segments are the same in both columns; only the order changes. With Nagle, the body waits behind the header's ACK, and that ACK waits 40 ms on the server's delayed-ACK timer. With TCP_NODELAY, the body follows 36 microseconds after the header, the server has the whole request, and its ACK and reply go at once.

worked.title: Find the stall in a capture

steps.say: Record the demo with tcpdump, a program that prints every packet, and print one connection with -ttt, which shows the time since the previous line. Pick any request after the first. Here the client's header, bytes 113 to 124, goes out the moment the program writes it: nothing was unacknowledged.
steps.code:
tcpdump -r n.pcap -nn -ttt port 55374

00:00:00.000080 55374 > 40069: [P.] seq 113:125, ack 3, length 12

steps.say: The next line is the server's ACK of the header, 40.7 ms later. The server's kernel had 12 bytes of a 112-byte request and nothing to send back, so it held the ACK for the delayed-ACK timer, hoping to put it on an answer.

41 microseconds after that ACK, the body leaves. The program wrote it long before, but Nagle kept it in the client's kernel because the header was unacknowledged. Now the server has the whole request, so it ACKs at once and replies.

Check the arithmetic against the demo's own numbers. 49 requests stalled for about 41 ms each, which is 2 seconds, and the run reported 2,065 ms for 50. The same pattern across a 20 ms round trip costs two round trips plus the timer, 80 ms instead of 20. The lab's writeWriteRead works out exactly that.
steps.code:
49 x 41 ms ~= 2,010 ms    measured: all 50 took 2065 ms
with TCP_NODELAY:          all 50 took 14 ms

across 20 ms RTT:  Nagle 2 x 20 + 40 = 80 ms   TCP_NODELAY 20 ms

lab.title: A congestion window simulator and a Nagle model
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 15 fail for now. WriteWriteRead.kt is finished: it times one write-write-read request using your NagleSender.
In Reno.kt, write onAck, onTripleDuplicateAck and onTimeout, a few lines each. The first five tests in RenoTest check slow start, halving, the exact +1 per round trip and the restart after a timeout.

In Sawtooth.kt, write sawtooth: the stepper's rules as a loop. The test expects the stepper's numbers, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 80, 81 and so on, and an average near 75. Then write cubicWindow, one line from the formula in its KDoc (the comment above the function).
In NagleSender.kt, write write and onAck. Run NagleTest until all its tests pass, including the 40 ms stall on 127.0.0.1 and the 80 ms one across a 20 ms round trip.
hints: Slow start is one line: cwnd += 1 per ACK. The doubling comes from getting cwnd ACKs every round trip, not from anything in onAck.
For congestion avoidance, count ACKs in the private acked field and add one segment when the count reaches cwnd. cwnd += 1.0 / cwnd on a Double drifts, and the tests expect exact whole numbers.
In sawtooth, read reno.cwnd once at the start of a round, record it, and use that same value for both the loss check and the number of ACKs.
kotlin.math.cbrt and pow are all cubicWindow needs. (-2.0).pow(3) is -8.0, so the curve works before k too.

Give NagleSender one private flush() that both write and onAck call, so the rule lives in one place: with noDelay or nothing unacknowledged, send everything in pieces of at most mss; otherwise send only full mss pieces.

drill.title: Three numbers in your head
drill.prompt: No tools. (a) How many bytes must be in flight to move 200 Mbit/s across a 40 ms round trip, and how many 1,448-byte segments is that? (b) A Reno sender on a path that holds 120 segments has settled into its sawtooth. Between which windows does it swing, and what's its average? (c) A client does write-write-read with Nagle on, across a 10 ms round trip, to a server whose delayed ACK waits 40 ms. How long does one request take, and how long with TCP_NODELAY? Then name the two places the bytes wait during the stall.

answer.html:
(a) BDP = 200,000,000 / 8 x 0.040 = 1,000,000 bytes, about 1 MB
    1,000,000 / 1,448 = about 690 segments in flight

(b) it loses at 121 (one more than the path holds), halves to 60,
    then +1 per round trip back to 121: swings 60..121, average about 90
    (three quarters of the top, the same as 75 out of 100 in the stepper)

(c) Nagle on:  header out at 0, delayed ACK leaves the server at 5 + 40 ms,
               reaches the client at 50, body arrives at 55, reply at 60 ms
               = 2 x RTT + 40 = 60 ms
    TCP_NODELAY: header and body together, reply after one round trip = 10 ms

    The body waits in the client's kernel (Nagle);
    the ACK it needs waits in the server's kernel (delayed ACK).

recap: A sender can have at most one window of bytes unacknowledged, so one connection moves at most one window per round trip. Filling a line needs bandwidth x round trip in flight, the bandwidth-delay product.
Flow control: the receive window is the free space in the receiver's buffer. A slow reader shrinks it to zero, and the sender's write() blocks. Recv-Q and Send-Q in ss show where the bytes wait.

Congestion control: the sender's own window starts at 10 segments, doubles each round trip in slow start, grows by one above ssthresh, and halves on loss. Linux uses CUBIC, which cuts to 70%. Loss is costly: 1% loss made a 10 MB download take about 20 s instead of 2.
Nagle holds small writes while data is unacknowledged, and the delayed ACK holds ACKs for at least 40 ms on Linux. Write-write-read hits both: write once, or set TCP_NODELAY.

The limit: windows let a connection fill a long path, but they can't shorten the round trip. Every request still waits at least one, a new connection starts in slow start, and one lost packet holds up everything behind it.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why the nightly copy to a backup computer 90 ms away crawls at 5 Mbit/s on a 1 Gbit/s line, while the same copy inside one building is fast. Explain what limits a single TCP connection, what the receive window and the congestion window each do, and what you'd check first.
explain.answer: A TCP sender can only have one window of bytes unacknowledged at a time, so a connection moves at most one window per round trip. Inside one building the round trip is under a millisecond, so even a small window is fast. At 90 ms, 5 Mbit/s means about 56 KB per round trip, which looks like a 64 KB window. Two things set the window. The receiver announces how much free buffer it has, which is flow control. If either side set a small socket buffer, or a firewall stripped the window-scaling option so the window can't pass 64 KB, we're stuck there. The sender also keeps a congestion window, its guess of what the path can carry: it starts at 10 segments, doubles each round trip and halves when packets are lost. So loss on the line would also keep it low, but that usually shows as a speed that jumps around. I'd check the SYNs in a capture for wscale on both sides, run ss -ti during the copy to see the window, rwnd_limited and resends, and look for any code that sets SO_RCVBUF. To fill 1 Gbit/s at 90 ms, we'd need about 11 MB in flight.

deeper.html:
Don't set socket buffers by hand. An explicit SO_RCVBUF or SO_SNDBUF turns off Linux's autotuning for that socket, and it's capped by net.core.rmem_max and wmem_max (212,992 bytes by default), as the first Try it showed. Autotuning grows the receive buffer up to the last number in tcp_rmem (6 MB in the lab box) as the measured bandwidth-delay product requires. A classic case is Kafka, a program that passes messages between programs: its consumer asks for a 64 KB receive buffer by default (receive.buffer.bytes = 65536), so a reader 70 ms away gets about 1 MB a second per connection however big the line is. Setting it to -1 hands the choice back to the kernel.

Batching on purpose. Kafka's producer settings linger.ms and batch.size are Nagle's idea done deliberately, in the program: wait a few milliseconds on purpose to fill a batch. Its client then sets TCP_NODELAY, so the kernel doesn't add a second wait on top.

A pooled connection forgets its speed. With net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle = 1, the default, Linux shrinks the congestion window of a connection that has been idle for longer than its retransmission timeout. So the first burst after a quiet minute starts slowly again. Linux also remembers the last ssthresh and round trip per destination between connections (ip tcp_metrics show), which is why the third Try it flushes them first.

How a sender times out. The retransmission timeout (RFC 6298) starts at 1 second and is then worked out from measured round trips: a smoothed average plus four times their variation, with a floor (200 ms on Linux). Every timeout in a row doubles it. That's the same back-off that UDP and the sockets API built by hand.

BBR in one paragraph. Loss-based algorithms such as CUBIC only back off once a queue overflows. So on links with big buffers they keep the queue full and add delay, which is called bufferbloat. BBR estimates the bottleneck bandwidth (the best delivery rate recently seen) and the shortest round trip, and sends at about that rate, cycling slightly above and below it to keep probing. Its first version could take more than its share of a link from CUBIC connections and ignored loss up to a point; later versions react to loss too, and the third is still an IETF draft. On a kernel built with it, sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr switches new connections, or a program can choose per socket.

Corking and low-water marks. Linux has TCP_CORK, the opposite of TCP_NODELAY: hold everything until the cork is pulled, used by servers that send headers and then a file. It also has autocorking, which merges small writes on a socket while its earlier packets are still queued inside the machine. TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT limits how much unsent data sits in the send buffer, which keeps delays low for web servers that send many streams at once and want to change their order quickly.
